claims.text: Running a compiled program asks the operating system to create a process that has its own memory, its own place in the code it is working through, and an id.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/threading/threads-and-threading ('a process is an executing program'); garbage-collection/fundamentals ('its own, separate virtual address space')

claims.text: Each process gets its own memory, so one process cannot read another process's variables; sharing between processes happens only when a program explicitly asks the operating system for it.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals (separate address space per process); dotnet/standard/io/memory-mapped-files (explicit OS facility for sharing)

claims.text: A process keeps running after the terminal that started it returns to the prompt — at stage-0 the Đơn Hàng example system keeps serving its pages after scripts/up.sh returns — and it produces no output unless the program writes some.
claims.source_hint: Docker docs, detached mode ('-d' runs the container in the background and returns you to the prompt); examples/don-hang/scripts/up.sh runs docker compose up -d --build --wait

claims.text: A process ends on its own — its main function returns, or it asks to end — or it crashes, or something outside it asks the operating system to stop it; whoever started it can read one number saying which.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/program-structure/main-command-line, 'Main() return values'; Environment.Exit for 'asks to end'; the stopped case rests on the captured run (143)

claims.text: By convention an exit code of 0 means the program succeeded and any other value means it failed.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/program-structure/main-command-line: 'A return value of 0 usually means success, and a nonzero value means there's an error'

claims.text: In .NET 10, System.Diagnostics.Process.GetCurrentProcess() returns a Process for the currently running process, and its Id property is the process id given by the operating system.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.Diagnostics.Process.GetCurrentProcess and Process.Id; CA1837 describes the same pair

claims.text: In .NET 10, Environment.ProcessPath returns the path of the executable file that started the current process.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.Environment.ProcessPath; CA1839 and the single-file deployment overview say the same

claims.text: The operating system decides an id when it creates a process, so you cannot count on two runs of the same file getting the same id — while the path of the started file does not change between runs.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference, Process.Id Remarks: an id is unique only while the process runs and can be reused later; outputs/unstable.regex masks the sleep pid, not the path

claims.text: ps -o pid=,args= -p <ids> prints only the process id and the command line of the processes whose ids are given, with no header line.
claims.source_hint: ps(1) manual: -o with the empty header suffix '=' and -p to select by id; verified by running it in the stage-0 lab box (procps from lab/Dockerfile): two lines, no header

claims.text: Inside the stage-0 lab box, kill with no signal argument asks the operating system to stop the process, and the script then reads 143 for it — a fixed number that marks that kind of stop, not a value the stopped process chose.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:15-16 and outputs/stage-0/.../list-processes.txt:4; 143 = 128 + 15; verified for the stage-0 lab box only (see open_questions)

claims.text: At stage-0, scripts/computer/list-processes.sh prints two sleep processes alive at once and then the numbers 143, 0 and 3.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/outputs/stage-0/scripts/computer/list-processes.txt, captured and compared by the example repository's CI

claims.text: A script can read the exit code of the thing that finished last through the special parameter $?, which is how it decides whether that thing worked.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Special Parameters': $? expands to the exit status of the last executed foreground pipeline; verified by the captured run (143 and 3 both printed through $?)

claims.text: The id a process reports about itself is the same id a system tool such as ps lists that process under while it is alive.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference, Process.Id Remarks: 'Until the process terminates, the process identifier uniquely identifies the process throughout the system'

claims.text: In list-processes.sh the numbers 0 and 3 come from two endings the script produces for itself, not from two further programs it starts.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:20-21 — ( exit 0 ) and ( exit 3 ) are subshells; the only programs it starts are the two sleeps, stopped on line 15

claims.text: At stage-0, scripts/computer/list-processes.sh only runs while what scripts/up.sh starts is up, so the example system must be running before step 2 of Try it.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/scripts/computer/list-processes.sh:5 re-executes through scripts/lab-run.sh:18 (docker compose exec -T lab), which only attaches to an already running service

claims.text: In the stage-0 lab box, & at the end of a command starts that program and lets the script carry on without waiting for it.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Lists of Commands': a command ending in & runs asynchronously and the shell does not wait for it; verified in the stage-0 lab box (both sleeps alive at once)

claims.text: In the stage-0 lab box, $! is the process id of the last program the script started with &; a subshell such as ( exit 3 ) does not set it.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Special Parameters': $! is the process id of the job last put in the background; verified by the two ids list-processes.sh prints for the two sleeps

claims.text: In the stage-0 lab box, wait <id> waits for a program the script started and yields its exit code; || runs the command after it only when the preceding exit code is not 0, and && only when it is 0.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Job Control Builtins' (wait) and 'Lists of Commands' (&& / || as AND-OR lists); the captured run: || printed 143 and 3, && printed after ( exit 0 )

claims.text: In the stage-0 lab box, the 2>/dev/null on the two wait lines discards the warning message printed on the error stream when a program the script started is stopped from outside.
claims.source_hint: Bash Reference Manual, 'Redirections' (2> redirects the error stream) and 'Job Control' (jobs ended abnormally are reported); verified with and without it in the stage-0 lab box

claims.text: In .NET 10, Environment.CurrentDirectory is the working directory of the current process, which is not necessarily the folder the started executable is in.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com .NET API reference: System.Environment.CurrentDirectory; compare Environment.ProcessPath (CA1839), which is the executable's own path

claims.text: A program that starts another program can learn how that program ended from its exit code without reading any of its output, but only if it asks for that number; a starter that never asks carries on regardless of the failure.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/fundamentals/program-structure/main-command-line ('send status information to other programs or scripts'); list-processes.sh sees 143 only via wait

repo_changes_needed.need: Replace the two lines using System.Diagnostics.Process.GetCurrentProcess() and process.Id with a single Console.WriteLine using Environment.ProcessId. Technical review (minor, section 5): CA1837 is enabled by default in .NET 10 as a suggestion against GetCurrentProcess().Id, the Process instance the sample creates is never disposed, and the sample already uses the sibling Environment.ProcessPath that CA1839 recommends, so the file teaches the discouraged half of a pair it otherwise uses correctly. Until the repository changes, the lesson describes the call without recommending it; after the change, the prose sentence becomes 'Environment.ProcessId is the number the operating system assigned to this process', the quoted line range shifts by one, and claim 6 is replaced.

open_questions: Claims 9, 10, 12, 16, 17, 18 and 19 rest on the stage-0 lab box only: content/versions.yaml pins neither a shell nor procps, so 143 (the 128+signal convention), $?, $!, &, wait, ||, && and the ps flags have no pinned version key. Technical review (minor, section 0) asks for a `shell` key (bash 5.3.9 in the lab image, check: bash --version) and optionally a `procps` key in content/versions.yaml, listed in this lesson's versions_used and set as version_key on those claims, so an image bump triggers the re-review that versions.yaml's policy requires. Not applied here: content/versions.yaml is a source-of-truth file this lesson may not edit on its own.

Junior review (minor, section 3) asks for all four Core concepts terms to be bolded or none. Neither is allowed: prompt 02 requires every vocab term (here `process`) to be bolded exactly once in Core concepts and forbids bold anywhere else. Left as is; `program`, `process id` and `exit code` are not glossary terms, so they are plain words the section defines. If the confusion is real, the fix belongs in the outline (add them to `vocab` and to glossary.yaml), not in this lesson.
